paragraphs: Use the sections that help you. This is a guide to describing situations, not a test of whether your experience or interpretation is true. The same material is available on phones and larger screens.

sections.title: What counts as an observation
sections.description: Describe the event, then add what it meant to you.

items: Describe actions, words, and outcomes you noticed. In behavioral recording, observable actions are described so another observer could recognize what happened [1].
Add the time, setting, or people when those details help place an event. Professional direct-observation guidance also records context alongside the specific behavior [2].
A thought or feeling can belong in the same account. For example: “She closed her laptop while I was speaking. I felt dismissed and wondered if she wanted the discussion to end.”
You do not need a number or exact quote for every observation. An estimate or a note that you are unsure is better than invented precision.

content.html: Both can stay. A description of what happened and an interpretation of what it meant are different kinds of information. One does not cancel the other.

sections.title: Why a word may be highlighted
sections.description: An invitation to add detail, not a correction.

items: “Always” or “never” can cover many events. You might add the dates, frequency, or one example you remember.
Words like “rude,” “unfair,” or “careless” may express an important judgment. You can keep the word and describe the particular words or actions behind it.
“On purpose” describes an interpretation of intent. If helpful, name the actions or statements that led you to that interpretation.
Words about harm, coercion, or pressure are not treated as unreal. Adding context should not erase what you experienced.
You can ignore a prompt that does not fit. The app checks wording patterns locally; it cannot establish what actually happened.

sections.title: From broad wording to specific detail
sections.description: The second version adds context without declaring the first false.

items.observation: “In the past two weeks, you arrived 5–15 minutes after our agreed time on three occasions.”
items.why: Adds a timeframe and count. You can still explain how those occasions affected you.

items.observation: “Janice logged 62 on-site hours this week, including Saturday.”
items.why: Names the hours and period being described. Whether that is too much remains a separate judgment.

items.evaluation: “He left the party to hurt me.”
items.observation: “He left at 9:10 p.m. without saying goodbye. I felt hurt and wondered whether it was deliberate.”
items.why: Records the action and preserves the feeling and question about intent.

items.observation: “During the 2:00–2:15 agenda item, you spoke twice while I was talking.”
items.why: Names what occurred. The speaker can still describe why those interruptions felt rude.

sections.title: When an exact record matters
sections.description: Methods used in professional behavioral observation.

content.text: The ideas below are mainly for ongoing records, team observations, or research. They are not requirements for a personal journal.

items: An operational definition describes a specific action so observers know what counts. Include examples and non-examples when the boundary could be unclear [1].
Frequency means how many times something happens; duration is how long it lasts; latency is the time between a specified event and an action. Choose a measure that fits what you are tracking [3].

ABC notes record what occurred before an action (antecedent), the action (behavior), and what followed (consequence). They can help examine patterns across events, but a single ABC note does not prove what caused an action [4].

When multiple people record the same behavior, interobserver agreement checks how closely their records match. Agreement is a measure of consistency, not proof that every recorded judgment is correct. Research on behavioral studies also emphasizes the importance of checking whether procedures were carried out as intended [5].

sections.title: What concrete detail can and cannot do
sections.description: A clearer record, not a guaranteed outcome.

content.text: A time, quote, count, or description of an action can help you revisit a particular event and show someone else the details you are referring to. You can add those details without giving up the words you use for its impact.

More details do not guarantee that two people will remember an event the same way or agree about its meaning. When you are tracking behavior repeatedly, clear descriptions can make later comparisons more consistent; they do not determine motivation on their own.

sections.title: Limits to remember
sections.description: Use concrete details as information, not a verdict.

items: Memory is incomplete and can change. Record exact words promptly when they matter, but mark estimates or uncertainty rather than inventing precision.
Two people can notice different parts of the same situation. Context, language, culture, access, and perspective can affect the resulting accounts.
A person's intent may not be directly observable. You can describe the evidence for a conclusion without presenting that conclusion as a measured fact.
This tool is not a clinical assessment, legal standard, credibility test, or requirement for being believed.
